readerTitle: Where a hotel stay really goes wrong
caseNote: 가상 사례 (호텔 그룹의 고객 경험팀, 가구 소매업체의 배송팀) · 실제 기업이나 수치 없음
insight: 고객 경험을 고칠 때는 가장 눈에 띄는 곳이 아니라 여정 전체를 그린 뒤 결과를 좌우하는 몇 순간에 집중한다.
misconception: 호텔 경험은 객실이 결정하므로 객실에 투자하면 평가가 오른다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨: 고객 여정(CUS-08-01), 진실의 순간(CUS-08-02)
모든 사례와 상황은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 이 레슨의 모든 장면(40개 호텔 그룹, 리뷰 내용, 가구 배송)은 설명용 가상 사례이며 실제 통계나 기업 사실을 쓰지 않았습니다. 수치를 추가하지 않았는지 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.
관련 레슨 CUS-08-01, CUS-08-02의 정의 및 용어와 이 레슨의 표현(customer journey, moments of truth)이 일치하는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Where a hotel stay really goes wrong
body: A guest spends maybe nine hours asleep in a hotel room. But the stay started days earlier with a booking email, and it ends days later with a credit card statement.
Most hotels pour money into the room. Many bad reviews start somewhere else.

image.label: A hotel stay drawn as a long path, with the room as one small stop
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 휴대폰 예약 화면에서 시작해 공항, 로비, 객실, 조식, 체크아웃, 카드 명세서로 이어지는 긴 길. 객실은 길 중간의 작은 점 하나로만 표현. 실제 호텔 로고나 브랜드 사용 금지.

cards.title: One budget, forty hotels.
body: You lead the guest experience team at a group of 40 mid-range hotels. Review scores are flat. Finance gives you one budget for one big improvement this year.

options.text: Refresh the rooms: new beds, better showers
options.feedback: Rooms matter, and it's the obvious bet. But you'd be spending the whole budget before knowing whether rooms are what guests actually complain about.

options.text: Map a full stay from the guest's side, then fund the weakest step
options.feedback: This is the **customer journey** at work. Seeing every step, from booking to the final bill, shows where the problems really sit before you spend.

options.text: Add a free welcome drink at every hotel
options.feedback: Cheap and pleasant. But a nice drink rarely makes up for a step that's broken earlier or later in the stay.

cards.title: The complaints weren't about the rooms.
body: Your team reads a year of reviews and sorts each complaint by step in the stay.
list: **Arrival and check-in:** long waits, rooms not ready
**Checkout and after:** surprise charges on the bill
cards.callout: Two steps nobody owned end to end held most of the anger.
cards.softwareNote: A software sign-up has the same shape: ad, sign-up form, first login, first bill. Complaints often cluster where one team hands off to another.

cards.title: Which moment do you fix first?
body: Check-in has many small problems. You can fix one properly this quarter.

options.text: A guest arrives at 11 p.m. after a delayed flight, and the room isn't ready
options.feedback: A tired guest with no backup plan is a **moment of truth**: a short moment that sets their whole view of you. Get it right and they forgive a lot.

options.text: Guests wait four minutes at a busy desk at 3 p.m.
options.feedback: Worth improving, but a short wait in daylight rarely decides how someone feels about the whole stay.

options.text: The lobby music is too loud
options.feedback: Easy to fix and easy to notice. It's also unlikely to shape the stay, so it can eat your quarter without moving reviews.

cards.title: Plan for the worst version of the moment.
body: The team writes down what the late, tired guest needs: a person who expects them, a room or a clear alternative, and an apology that doesn't need a manager.
So night staff get a short script, a held-back room for emergencies, and permission to offer a free breakfast without asking anyone. The fix is mostly rules, not renovation.

image.label: Night desk clerk handing a key to a tired traveler with a suitcase
image.brief: 밤 11시 호텔 프런트. 지친 여행객이 캐리어를 끌고 들어오고, 직원이 미소 지으며 열쇠와 작은 조식 쿠폰을 건넴. 시계가 11시를 가리킴. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: A map crosses team lines.
body: Front desk owns check-in. Housekeeping owns room readiness. Finance owns the bill. The weakest steps often sit between teams, so nobody feels responsible.

A journey map only helps if someone owns each handoff. Also, build it from what guests did and said, not from what staff assume. And don't try to fix every step at once. Pick the few that decide the stay.

cards.title: Now it's a furniture store.
body: You run operations for a regional furniture retailer. Showroom reviews are great. Overall reviews are poor. Customers wait three weeks for a sofa, then get a four-hour delivery window.

options.text: Redesign the showroom to impress buyers even more
options.feedback: The showroom already works. Improving it ignores the **journey** after the purchase, where the trouble shows up.

options.text: Map the steps after payment and fix the delivery day
options.feedback: The map shows the wait and the delivery. The day a stranger carries a sofa into someone's home is the **moment of truth**: text updates and careful crews pay off here.

options.text: Offer a discount to customers who complain
options.feedback: It calms some people down. But it pays for the problem again and again instead of fixing the step that causes it.

cards.title: Map the whole path, then fix the moments that decide it.
body: You used two ideas here. The **customer journey** showed where problems really sat. **Moments of truth** showed which of them to fix first.
**Try it today:** write the steps a customer goes through with you, from first contact to the final bill. Circle the one where a tired or worried customer would judge you hardest.
